# Conclusion

## Research Journey

Over several years of surveying technology professionals and writing State of DevOps Reports with Puppet, the authors researched technology transformations, published peer-reviewed findings, and worked with colleagues assessing and transforming their own organizations. Breakthrough discoveries revealed relationships between delivery performance, technical practices, cultural norms, and organizational performance.

## Software Delivery Performance

Since nearly every company relies on software, delivery performance is critical to any organization. It is affected by leadership, tools, automation, and a culture of continuous learning and improvement. The ability to deliver quality software at high tempo with stability is a key value driver and differentiator for all organizations, regardless of size or industry vertical.

## Book Structure

Part I presented research findings on why software delivery performance drives organizational performance—profitability, productivity, market share, efficiency, effectiveness, customer satisfaction, and mission goals. Part II summarized the science behind the research, including design decisions and analysis methods. Part III addressed organizational change management through a contributed chapter by colleagues Steve Bell and Karen Whitley Bell, presenting what following the outlined capabilities and practices looks like and what it can provide for innovative organizations.

## Transformation and Capability Development

High performance cannot be bought or copied. Organizations must develop their own capabilities pursuing a path fitting their particular context and goals. This requires sustained effort, investment, focus, and time, but the results are worth it.

# Conclusion

## Research Journey and Key Findings

Over several years of surveying technology professionals and writing State of DevOps Reports with Puppet, the authors discovered what makes high-performing teams and organizations. Their research included technology transformations, peer-reviewed publications, and collaboration with colleagues assessing and transforming their own organizations. The breakthrough discoveries revealed relationships between delivery performance, technical practices, cultural norms, and organizational performance.

## Software Delivery Performance as Critical Value Driver

One finding proved consistently true: since nearly every company relies on software, delivery performance is critical to any organization. Software delivery performance is affected by many factors including leadership, tools, automation, and a culture of continuous learning and improvement. The ability to deliver quality software at high tempo with stability is a key value driver and differentiator for all organizations, regardless of size or industry vertical.

## Book Structure and Contributions

Part I presented research findings, starting with why software delivery performance matters and how it drives organizational performance measures—profitability, productivity, market share, efficiency, effectiveness, customer satisfaction, and mission goals. Part II summarized the science behind the research, including design decisions and analysis methods. Part III addressed organizational change management through a contributed chapter by colleagues Steve Bell and Karen Whitley Bell, presenting what following the outlined capabilities and practices looks like and what it can provide for innovative organizations.

## Transformation and Capability Development

The authors hope the book helps readers identify areas for improving technology, business processes, work culture, and improvement cycles. The research is unequivocal: high performance cannot be bought or copied. Organizations must develop their own capabilities pursuing a path fitting their particular context and goals. This requires sustained effort, investment, focus, and time, but the results are worth it.

# Chapter 1 - Accelerate

Organizations must accelerate software delivery, engage with markets to detect demand, anticipate compliance changes, and respond to risks. Software is the key differentiator—banks trade faster through technology, retailers win through superior service, and government serves citizens more effectively. Research by Bessen (2017) and McAfee and Brynjolfsson (2008) confirms the strategic use of technology explains revenue and productivity gains more than M&A or entrepreneurship. These capabilities emerge from the DevOps movement, developed to solve the problem of building secure, resilient, rapidly evolving distributed systems at scale. Even large enterprises with decades-old technologies gain significant benefits through adoption.

A Forrester report (2017) found 31% of organizations are not using essential practices like continuous integration and delivery, Lean, and collaborative culture. A Gartner study shows 47% of CEOs face board pressure for digital transformation. Organizations also overestimate their progress—the gap between executive and practitioner estimates highlights both untapped potential and the need for accurate measurement. If practitioner estimates are more accurate (being closer to the work), the potential for value delivery is greater than executives realize.

Leaders should focus on capabilities rather than maturity models. Maturity models assume arrival at a static "done" state, use lock-step prescriptions that ignore context differences, measure technical install base without tying to outcomes (vanity metrics), and don't account for changing landscapes. Capability models enable continuous improvement, allow customization to team context, are outcome-based, and adapt to dynamically changing environments. The highest performers never consider themselves mature or finished.

Research identified 24 key capabilities that drive software delivery performance and organizational outcomes like profitability and market share. Notably, factors like application age, who performs deployments, or whether a CAB exists do not predict performance—the research controlled for these variables. High performers achieve 46× more frequent deployments, 440× faster lead time, 170× faster recovery, and 5× lower change failure rates than low performers. The gap for stability widened in 2017, suggesting low performers increased tempo without building quality, while high performers achieve both speed and stability. These capabilities apply across all organization types, sizes, industries, and technology stacks.

# Chapter 1 - Accelerate

## The Imperative to Accelerate

"Business as usual" is no longer sufficient for competitive survival. Organizations across industries are shifting from large projects with long lead times toward small teams working in short cycles with user feedback. To remain competitive, organizations must accelerate: delivery of goods and services, market engagement to detect customer demand, anticipation of compliance changes, and response to risks including security threats.

## Software as Strategic Differentiator

Software sits at the center of this acceleration. Banks deliver value through faster, more secure trading and new customer channels. Retailers compete through superior selection, service, and seamless online/offline experiences—all technology-enabled. Research by James Bessen (2017) found that strategic use of technology explains revenue and productivity gains more than mergers and acquisitions or entrepreneurship. McAfee and Brynjolfsson (2008) established a link between technology and profitability.

## DevOps Transformation

DevOps practices are transforming industries. Notable examples include web-scale tech giants (Netflix, Amazon, Google, Facebook) and traditional enterprises (Capital One, Target, US Federal Government's Technology Transformation Service and US Digital Service). However, a 2017 Forrester report found 31% of the industry still lacks widely-accepted practices like continuous integration/delivery, Lean, and collaborative culture. Gartner found 47% of CEOs face board pressure to digitally transform. Organizations consistently overestimate their progress, with executives especially prone to overestimation compared to practitioners.

## Focus on Capabilities, Not Maturity

The authors argue capability models outperform maturity models for four reasons: maturity models treat transformation as reaching an end state rather than continuous improvement; they prescribe lock-step linear formulas rather than allowing customized approaches; they measure technical proficiency without tying to outcomes (vanity metrics); and they define static levels rather than adapting to changing environments. Capability models are multidimensional, outcome-based, and dynamic.

## Evidence-Based Findings

Surprisingly, factors that do NOT predict performance include: application age/technology (mainframe vs. greenfield), whether operations or development teams perform deployments, and whether a change approval board (CAB) is implemented. The research identified 24 key capabilities that drive software delivery and organizational performance.

## Performance Gaps

2017 data shows high performers versus low performers have: 46x more frequent code deployments, 440x faster lead time from commit to deploy, 170x faster mean time to recover from downtime, and 5x lower change failure rate. The gap in stability metrics widened from 2016, suggesting low performers increased tempo without building in quality. High performers achieve both speed and stability by building quality into the process.
